claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA has a density below 6 g/cm3.
The as-solidified alloy initially consists largely of a homogeneous metastable solid solution.
The as-solidified alloy contains minor intermetallic phases.
Post-solidification thermal aging or corrosive exposure drives Mg diffusion out of the metastable solid-solution matrix.
Diffusing Mg segregates into localized intermetallic precipitates or grain-boundary phases.
Mg segregation produces compositional and microstructural heterogeneity.
Mg-rich segregated regions act as localized galvanic-interaction sites during corrosion.
Localized galvanic interactions caused by Mg segregation promote localized corrosion such as pitting.
Mg segregation alters the morphology and composition of the high-temperature oxide scale.
The altered oxide scale changes oxidation resistance relative to the as-solidified baseline.
Aged or environmentally exposed samples will have different corrosion performance from as-solidified samples.
The change in oxidation resistance may be either beneficial or detrimental.
The proposed pathway is expected to operate during oxidation at approximately 600–800°C and corrosion in chloride-based electrolytes.
Constituent stabilizers can prevent Mg segregation and thereby suppress the proposed pathway.
The proposed pathway may not operate outside the tested thermal and corrosive exposure ranges.
A controlled comparison of as-solidified and treated samples can test for Mg segregation, phase formation, corrosion changes, and oxide-scale changes.
Failure to observe significant changes in Mg segregation, microstructure, corrosion behavior, or oxide-scale properties relative to baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
